abstract: The U.S. Entity List restricts targeted firms' access to critical inputs and technologies, which can affect their investment decisions. Using firm‐level data from Bureau van Dijk's Orbis and Zephyr databases from 2011 to 2023, we examine the impact of the U.S. Entity List on the mergers and acquisitions (M&A) activities of Chinese firms. We find that U.S. Entity List inclusion has a negative and significant impact on the number and value of targeted firms' M&A deals. Our results are robust to various confounding factors, alternative M&A measures, and estimation methods. The effect is heterogeneous: the decline in M&A activity is less pronounced among firms with lower reliance on U.S. imports and among firms located in eastern regions. The mechanism analysis shows that the Entity List has increased uncertainty and intensified firms' financial constraints. Moreover, the inclusion reduces the share of M&A in the Western bloc countries. Our findings offer valuable insights for firms and policymakers navigating the challenges of rising protectionism and geopolitical risks.

abstract: This paper examines how countries can efficiently prepare for severe disruptions to international food supply. We frame national crisis preparedness as an insurance problem: a country determines the domestic capacity needed to meet nutritional needs if trade fails, while minimizing economic distortions in normal times. An optimization model, applied to Norway, identifies least-cost “crisis menus” based on domestic resources. Results show that preparedness can be achieved at an economic burden substantially lower than current self-sufficiency-oriented policies. The analysis highlights how national preparedness strategies can align with comparative advantage, suggesting how decentralized production capacity might support broader regional resilience.
title: National preparedness for food supply shocks: An economic efficiency approach

abstract: This paper uses a range of natural experiments to show how mispricing of climate risk in mortgages and property insurance creates large taxpayer exposures and leads to excess credit flows to risky areas. Our central finding is that the government-sponsored enterprises’ (GSEs) policies for evaluating property insurers are a crucial source of this mispricing. We assemble a comprehensive new dataset on both mortgages and insurance to analyze these dynamics in Florida from 2009-2018. We begin by documenting a breakdown in the quality of insurance provision, with new under-capitalized and under-diversified insurers dominating insurance markets. These fragile insurers have high rates of insolvency, which we show causally increases mortgage defaults after natural disasters. We find that the GSEs’ reliance on third-party ratings of insurers leads them to accept insurance from companies at high risk of insolvency without pricing for it. This creates large taxpayer exposures, with an estimated 25% of the GSEs’ expected losses in Florida coming from insurance fragility. Most starkly, we show that private lenders strategically respond to the GSE mispricing. Mortgage denial rates are sensitive to insurance quality in the jumbo segment where loans are retained, but not in the conforming segment where loans are offloaded to the GSEs. This suggests that, all else equal, fewer conforming mortgages would have been originated if lenders screened insurance fragility as they do in jumbos.
title: When Insurers Exit: Climate Losses, Fragile Insurers, and Mortgage Markets*

abstract: People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. We develop an attention-based framework for understanding why errors persist. When a person channels his attention through the lens of his potentially misspecified model, exposure to data is not the same as tracking the statistics necessary to tell him his model is wrong. A model is attentionally stable when the data the person deems relevant will, in the long run, fail to make the model look implausible. Models that erroneously rule things out—e.g., beliefs that a variable doesn’t matter or that a distinction doesn’t exist—tend to be attentionally stable because they divert attention away from data that would refute the models. Conversely, models that erroneously rule things in are less likely to be stable. Whether an error is discovered depends on the structure of the decision problem but is not tightly linked to its level of harm; arbitrarily costly errors can persist while trivially inexpensive ones may be detected. Nevertheless, no error is robust both to changes in the decision environment and to shocks that expand attention: every channeled-attention error is vulnerable to some perturbation that would reveal it. We use the framework to analyze the stability of psychological biases and empirical misconceptions, as well as to explain why fresh eyes catch mistakes, why people use overly coarse rather than overly fine categorizations, and why people recognize errors in others that they miss in themselves.
title: Channeled Attention and Stable Errors*

abstract: We examine how a profit-driven platform designs its recommender policies under varying privacy protection regimes. We demonstrate a functional equivalence between opt-out protection and unprotected privacy. Notably, granting consumers the autonomy to misrepresent personal data can compel the platform to distort recommendations, inadvertently harming both parties. When recommendations are purely informative, such privacy controls can deter personalization entirely. However, when recommendations also serve an allocative role—controlling product access—algorithmic discrimination may emerge, restricting the disadvantaged minority from valuable opportunities. These findings remain robust even with endogenous profit margins. This paper was accepted by Omar Besbes, revenue management and market analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05007 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Recommender Systems Under Privacy Protection

abstract: We conducted survey experiments to gather new data on uncertainty attitudes and subjective beliefs. Our survey targets a general population, focusing on health and financial decisions. We collect data on (i) individual attitudes toward risk and ambiguity, including individual-specific probability weighting and loss aversion, and (ii) individual probabilistic beliefs about events related to the decisions we consider. The joint availability of individual preference parameters and subjective beliefs allows us to study heterogeneity and cross-correlations across these parameters in depth and to estimate structural models of decision making under uncertainty that go beyond subjective expected utility. We find that both preferences and beliefs are highly heterogeneous. Compared with subjective expected utility, prospect theory combined with source-dependent probability weighting fits the data strictly better in some contexts and equally well in others. Prospect theory performs particularly well when the belief distribution is concentrated toward extreme values. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: A. Delavande acknowledges funding from the Economic and Social Research Council Research Centre on Micro-Social Change [Grants ES/L009153/1 and ES/S012486/1] and the National Institute on Aging [Grant P01AG008291]. J. Ganguli acknowledges research support from the Economic and Social Research Council [Grant ES/K00168X/1]. F. Mengel acknowledges support from the European Research Council [Grant DYNNET-805017]. Ethical approval was obtained by the Ethics Social Sciences subcommittee at the University of Essex in August 2015. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06232 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Uncertainty Attitudes, Subjective Beliefs, and Decisions Under Uncertainty

abstract: This paper exploits the 2014 U.S. Ebola outbreak as a natural experiment to examine how fear distorts mortgage credit allocation. We find a 3.8-percentage-point increase in mortgage denial rates for Black applicants during the outbreak, despite negligible infection risk. Approved Black borrowers have stronger credit profiles and lower default rates, yet are less likely to receive loan modifications when delinquent. These effects are absent in algorithm-driven FinTech lending and reverse quickly postoutbreak—patterns inconsistent with statistical discrimination. Robustness tests rule out alternative explanations related to political cycles, labor market impacts, applicant pool composition changes, and bank financial conditions. Consistent with diagnostic expectation theory, higher exposure to Ebola fear does not result in a significant learning effect during the COVID-19 pandemic. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal acknowledges the financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72495154]. Y. Lin gratefully acknowledges financial support from the NUS Research Grant [Grants A-8001725 and A-8004426]. R. Lu and X. Zhang acknowledge the financial support of the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 71903005, 72402005, and 72472001]. abstract: We investigate how long an insolvent debtor can avoid default when survival benefits creditors collectively, but individual creditors gain from early repayment. Standard theory predicts that debt is not rolled over and default is immediate. Previous experimental studies of related environments suggest that liquidation is delayed, and we confirm that pattern here. We then study how secondary markets affect outcomes. The duration of the credit pool is unaffected, but average net payoffs increase because claims are held longer before redemption. With markets, realized payoff dispersion is significantly higher. Prices do not predict liquidation timing but correlate with realized payoffs.
title: The role of financial markets in the unraveling of credit

abstract: Les enfants réfugiés nouvellement arrivés doivent-ils intégrer immédiatement le système scolaire ordinaire ou fréquenter d’abord des écoles séparées ? En prenant l’exemple des Pays-Bas, cet article montre que ce choix implique un compromis majeur à long terme : l’intégration directe réduit le niveau de réussite scolaire, mais elle favorise l’assimilation culturelle, telle que mesurée par le recours à la contraception hormonale chez les adolescentes. L’accès plus large, dans les écoles séparées, à des enseignants spécialisés dans l’enseignement de la langue maternelle à des locuteurs non natifs pourrait expliquer leur avantage sur le plan scolaire.
authors: Caterina Pavese, Simon ter Meulen, Ludger Woessmann
title: Scolarisation des enfants réfugiés : effets à long terme de l’intégration par rapport à la séparation

abstract: The global secular decline in long-term interest rates since the 1990s has been largely driven by cumulative yield changes during U.S. monetary policy announcement windows (FOMC windows). We document this FOMC-window effect for a group of ten major advanced economies. Based on a term structure model, we show that the effect operates through the expected path of future short-term interest rates rather than term premia. We further find that the global secular decline in interest rates has been concentrated in FOMC windows preceded by macroeconomic news. We interpret this pattern as a “Fed response to news” channel and provide empirical evidence to support this interpretation.
title: US monetary policy, macroeconomic news and the global secular decline of interest rates

abstract: The expansion of renewable energy across Europe increases the importance of cross-border electricity interconnections for system balancing, trade and energy security. Recent events, however, reveal the asymmetric vulnerabilities from interconnection disruptions faced by geopolitically exposed, peripheral, and import-dependent electricity markets. This article highlights the challenges posed by cross-border infrastructure fragility and uses the Baltic States—an electricity peninsula within the European system—as an illustrative case. Drawing on a price-zone–by-hour panel comprising a feasible control set of European electricity markets in 2024–2025, the study constructs credible counterfactuals for the Baltic States and exploits discontinuities in day-ahead electricity prices using three state-of-the-art econometric causal estimators. The results indicate that interruptions to cross-border electricity exchange generate substantial electricity price shocks. The EstLink 2 damage incident in December 2024 increased Baltic day-ahead electricity prices by approximately €30-40/MWh. The February 2025 desynchronization from the Russian-operated frequency area and the subsequent island-mode operation produced more variable estimates across specifications and estimators, but the effects remained consistently positive, statistically significant, and of a similar magnitude. The restoration of EstLink 2 in June 2025 generated effects of comparable magnitude with the expected opposite sign, further supporting the robustness of the estimated causal effects. These real-world stress tests underscore the heightened exposure of small, highly interconnected electricity systems to geopolitical shocks. We argue that European governance frameworks must more explicitly account for cross-border infrastructure risks and strengthen cooperative mechanisms to ensure the resilience of electricity transmission in an increasingly integrated, yet geopolitically vulnerable energy landscape.
title: Geopolitical exposure in cross-border electricity transmission: Evidence from Baltic desynchronization and interconnection disruptions

abstract: We examine a foreign innovator that makes a drastic innovation that would typically eliminate a domestic rival and create a monopoly. The domestic government's credible threat to nationalize the domestic rival stops this from happening. Rather than face the nationalized rival, the innovator licenses the domestic laggard, increasing domestic welfare. The equilibrium license is a two-part tariff. Adding an ad valorem royalty, making either firm a Stackelberg leader, or threatening only partial nationalization changes the composition of the license but not its form: it always combines a fixed fee with a royalty and always increases domestic welfare.
title: The Strategic Threat of Nationalizing a Laggard Domestic Firm

abstract: This paper estimates government consumption and investment multipliers for 18 low-income Sub-Saharan African (SSA) countries. We employ a Bayesian random effect panel vector autoregressive model, where a hierarchical approach allows the degree of heterogeneity in the coefficients to be determined within the inference procedure. This framework avoids imposing homogeneous slope restrictions and allows for country-specific estimates of fiscal multipliers. Findings show substantial heterogeneity across countries, with formal tests indicating that investment multipliers are often larger than consumption multipliers with high probability. An exploratory analysis of the relationship between multipliers and a set of potential determinants highlights the role of labour market slack, trade openness, and GDP per capita, while debt-to-GDP and informality emerge as additional determinants specific to investment multipliers.
title: Heterogeneous government consumption and investment multipliers in low-income Sub-Saharan Africa

abstract: This paper examines whether multinational supply chains improve energy efficiency in domestic firms. Our theoretical model predicts that foreign firms in upstream manufacturing and energy sectors increase the availability of high‐quality inputs, reducing energy intensity in downstream domestic firms. We test these predictions using data on Turkish manufacturing firms from 2010 to 2015. We find that domestic firms in sectors more likely to source manufacturing and energy inputs from foreign suppliers exhibit lower energy intensity. Results are robust to numerous sensitivity checks, including controls for firms' outsourcing and vertical‐integration strategies, and are supported by an instrumental‐variable approach. Consistent with the model, foreign presence in upstream sectors improves input quality, a key channel through which foreign direct investment enhances downstream firms' energy efficiency.
title: Energy efficiency gains from multinational supply chains: evidence from Turkey

abstract: We introduce macroeconomic forecasters as strategic agents who may bias their reports to influence their audience. We test the motives of forecasters using monthly forecaster‐level data around the Brexit referendum. To guide our analysis, we model the way in which a referendum voter forms expectations based on the reports of a politically motivated forecaster. The forecaster trades off its reputation for honesty against the opportunity to influence the vote. The model predicts that the forecaster lies selectively and continues to do so even after the referendum. Our analysis finds that forecasters exposed to financial losses from Brexit issued significantly less accurate GDP growth forecasts than others. The findings suggest that influential forecasters may strategically manipulate information when the stakes are high.
title: Biased forecasts and voting

abstract: We use merged registry data from two large Norwegian counties to examine how formalized behavioral grading affects in‐class grades in high school. Comparing students with similar performance on anonymously graded exams, we find that lower behavioral grades, especially for orderliness, significantly reduce in‐class academic evaluations. Males, students from low socio‐economic backgrounds, and those with immigrant backgrounds are more likely to receive lower behavioral grades, though the academic penalty is similar across groups. The results suggest that teachers place greater weight on organizational skills than on interpersonal behavior, raising concerns about the fairness of teacher‐assigned grades and the extent to which behavioral factors influence academic assessments.
title: Oh, behave! Determinants and consequences of behavioral grades in schools

abstract: Do depositors see state-owned banks as safer? The isolated, unexpected failure of Banco Santos, a private bank, in November 2004 raised the perceived risk of uninsured deposits in Brazil. Time deposits at state-owned banks grew 6.6 percentage points per month faster than at private banks, a gap of 56 percent after seven months. Excluding the largest banks leaves the estimate unchanged, separating ownership from too-big-to-fail size. Demand and savings deposits, whose clients were almost all fully insured, show no movement.
title: State ownership and deposit safety

abstract: Global energy enterprises are increasingly exposed to shocks that propagate across sectors, regions, and financial markets, yet aggregate market-level studies provide limited evidence on which firms transmit or absorb systemic risks. This study develops a firm-level multidimensional connectedness framework to examine risk spillovers among 50 representative oil, gas, and power enterprises from December 23, 2021 to June 30, 2026. Using daily stock-price data from Yahoo Finance, we construct return, volatility, skewness, and kurtosis risk measures through the GJR-SK model and estimate high-dimensional spillovers with an Elastic Net-VAR-based Diebold–Yilmaz and Barunik–Krehlik framework. The results show that global energy enterprises form a strongly connected risk network. Volatility is the most important channel of systemic spillover, while returns and kurtosis also display substantial connectedness; skewness spillovers are weaker but reveal selective asymmetric-risk transmission. Frequency decomposition indicates that spillovers are mainly short-term, although volatility contains a more persistent long-term component. Firm roles vary across risk dimensions and shock types: oil and gas majors dominate return and volatility transmission, utilities and infrastructure firms become important in uncertainty networks, and refining and downstream firms play central roles in tail-risk episodes. Event-window evidence further shows that the same firms can switch between transmitters and receivers under different shocks. These findings provide firm-level evidence for energy-finance systemic risk monitoring, portfolio risk management, and energy-security regulation.
title: Multidimensional time–frequency risk spillovers among global energy enterprises: Firm-level evidence from higher-moment connectedness

abstract: This study explores how heterogeneity within the consumer stakeholder group relates to discretionary firm sustainability investments. Specifically, how a greater presence of lower and middle income (LMI) customers coupled with a greater prosumer presence relates to utilities' sustainability investments in the empirical context of community solar. We find that utilities are more likely to make sustainability investments, the less their customer base is tilted toward LMI consumers, and the more prosumers are in their customer base, a finding supporting the notion that firms often underserve disadvantaged communities. We draw on comparative governance arguments to examine the boundary effect that customer heterogeneity may have on cooperatives' tendencies to address social imbalances and contrast for-profit utilities with cooperative utilities in the U.S. We find that customer heterogeneity by increasing coordination costs in cooperatives results in cooperatives prioritizing economic over social actions in the case of discretionary sustainability innovations, such as solar energy, that are ‘nice to have’, but not necessities for their members. We thus find that cooperative utilities behave similarly to for-profit utilities in the case of non-essential sustainability innovations such as community solar.
title: Consumer income heterogeneity and firm sustainability investments

abstract: Bitcoin has no contractual cash flow, yet its valuation depends on the services it provides and the infrastructure through which it is traded. We develop a structural framework with a money-in-utility fundamental, fixed Bitcoin supply, and a stablecoin-based settlement requirement. The requirement creates a shadow wedge in the household pricing condition, while a reserve-backed issuer supplies settlement balances and holds a small Bitcoin position. The calibration jointly matches aggregate Bitcoin valuation and the reported Bitcoin share of issuer reserves. Comparisons that remove the marginal settlement requirement but preserve the steady state show that settlement increases Bitcoin price sensitivity to productivity and monetary-policy shocks. Exogenous attention and turnover shift convenience demand, and turnover also changes required settlement balances. Fixed supply then links household demand to issuer portfolio adjustment. Under the assumed shock processes, productivity dominates Bitcoin-price variation, whereas turnover dominates settlement-balance variation. Attention and turnover have economically negligible effects on consumption, output and inflation, and their Bitcoin-price variance shares fall under proxy-based shock moments. The framework separates the convenience fundamental, the settlement user cost, and issuer portfolio demand within a unified account of Bitcoin valuation.
title: The settlement wedge in bitcoin valuation

abstract: I study the effect of firms’ defensive investment on aggregate total factor productivity (TFP) in a dynamic general-equilibrium model with heterogeneous firms, where incumbents can invest to deter both imitation and entry, while entrants either enter existing product markets or lead entirely new ones. I derive a decomposition of aggregate TFP into allocative and net technical efficiency, the latter capturing average firm-level productivity and variety. I calibrate the model to U.S. Compustat data to match the joint relationships between intangible investment, firm productivity, market share, and firm size. I find that defensive investment reduces aggregate TFP by 4 percent, primarily by lowering firm-level productivity, and that higher product variety partially offsets the loss—absent which the TFP cost would double. Firm-level evidence supports the model’s predictions.
journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

title: Blocking the Blockers? Defensive Investment and Aggregate Productivity

abstract: This paper studies the local and aggregate effects of cash transfers in developing countries, and how both change as the cash transfer program scales up. We build a two-region New Keynesian small open economy model and calibrate it to rich pre-treatment microdata from an ongoing cash transfer experiment in Malawi. The model implies a local GDP multiplier on temporary transfers of about one, which depends on price stickiness, the share of liquidity-constrained households, and home bias in consumption. Spillovers to the rest of the country are negative under Malawi’s restricted international capital mobility and parallel exchange rate regimes, as cash transfers appreciate the real exchange rate and reduce exports. Consequently, the aggregate GDP multiplier is less than the local multiplier. As the program scales up, the local multiplier converges toward the aggregate multiplier, so a scaled-up program may have smaller multipliers than micro-level estimates suggest. However, with unrestricted capital mobility, spillovers can be positive, especially under a fixed exchange rate. These results highlight the importance of the macroeconomic policy environment for aggregate multipliers and the effects of scaled-up transfer programs.
title: Cash transfers in developing countries: Local multipliers, aggregate effects, and external adjustment

abstract: This paper studies how occupational choice shapes life-cycle earnings growth and inequality, and how this margin changes the effects of progressive taxation. I focus on occupational technology exposure, measured as the intensity of information technology usage, and document its positive relationship with earnings. I develop a life-cycle model with a college decision, human capital investments, occupational choices, and incomplete markets. Results suggest occupational choice incentivizes human capital formation over the life-cycle and hence affects life-cycle earnings. In particular, it accounts for 42% of life-cycle earnings growth and 45% of inequality growth. Endogenous occupational choice also amplifies the distortionary effect of progressive taxation on earnings growth by 30% relative to a model without occupational choice. This amplification also leads to a larger decline in tax revenue and a larger welfare loss when tax progressivity increases.
title: Occupational choice, human capital formation and life-cycle earnings

abstract: The advantages of adaptive experiments have led to their rapid adoption in economics, other fields, and among practitioners. However, adaptive experiments pose challenges for causal inference. This note suggests a BOLS (batched ordinary least squares) test statistic for inference on treatment effects in adaptive experiments. The statistic provides a precision-equalizing aggregation of per-period treatment-control differences under heteroskedasticity. The combined test statistic is a linear combination of heteroskedastic per-period z -statistics and can be used to construct asymptotically valid confidence intervals. We provide simulation results comparing rejection rates in the typical case with few treatment periods and few (or many) observations per batch.
title: Inference for batched adaptive experiments

abstract: Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is a pathway for aviation decarbonization, but its green premium makes deployment dependent on government support. This study develops a two-stage Stackelberg game to examine how a limited public decarbonization budget should be allocated between SAF subsidies and high-speed rail (HSR) support. The model endogenizes the subsidy-induced reduction in aviation emissions intensity and its effect on air–rail price competition. Results show cleaner aviation reduces the environmental benefit of keeping HSR fares low to attract passengers. The HSR operator therefore raises its fare, causing passengers to shift back to aviation and potentially reducing emissions savings relative to a fixed-fare benchmark. This feedback is stronger when air and HSR are closer substitutes and the HSR operator places more weight on social welfare. When market feedback is sufficiently strong and SAF technological efficiency is low, it may offset the subsidy’s marginal emissions benefit. The marginal welfare effect of an initial reallocation towards SAF changes sign at a boundary marginal welfare threshold. When welfare is non-concave, however, this boundary condition does not determine the global optimum, which requires welfare comparisons over the full allocation range. These findings highlight the need to consider government budget allocation, HSR pricing, and modal shifts.
title: Do green subsidies always reduce emissions? Strategic pricing and abatement leakage in the air–rail market

abstract: This paper studies how policy-induced supply chain digitalization affects firm-level employment. We use China’s 2018 Supply Chain Innovation and Application pilot programme, under which central ministries designated a list of pilot firms required to digitalize their supply chain operations, as a quasi-natural experiment, and estimate difference-in-differences models on a panel of A-share listed firms over 2010–2024. Pilot designation raises firm employment by roughly 26 log points (about 29.6%) relative to non-pilot firms, an effect that emerges after 2018, persists over time, and survives an event-study analysis, randomization inference, alternative measures of supply chain digitalization, and robustness checks. Pilot firms also increase measured supply chain digitalization after designation. Consistent with the policy operating through firm expansion rather than labour substitution, policy-induced supply chain digitalization also increases patenting, total factor productivity, and operating revenue, and raises average wages for both ordinary employees and executives. The employment response is larger among firms that retain more earnings, face tighter financing constraints, and operate in more competitive industries, and it is amplified when firm-level and city-level pilots overlap. In contrast to the displacement fears surrounding automation, our results provide evidence that policy-induced digitalization of supply chain linkages expanded jobs and wages at targeted firms.

abstract: Stillwagon (this issue) tests extensively for structural breaks in a dynamic Taylor rule for US data and finds no breaks over 2001–2025, whether using Bai–Perron tests or multiplicative indicator saturation. The current paper complements and builds on Stillwagon by focusing on features specific to three Fed chairs (Bernanke, Yellen, and Powell) during 2006–2025, and on the zero lower bound. The Taylor rule is chair‐specific; and the zero lower bound affects the Taylor rule for Yellen's and Powell's tenures. These economically significant structural breaks are detectable by multiplicative indicator saturation that focuses on those features, whereas the broad‐spectrum multiplicative indicator saturation in Stillwagon misses these breaks. Such structural breaks limit the interpretability and usefulness of the Taylor rule for monetary policy.
journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics
title: Structural Breaks in the Taylor Rule

abstract: How does fiscal and administrative centralization affect the provision of public services? We address this question using a 2009 Vietnamese reform which dissolved elected district councils in some provinces and transferred authority to provincial bodies. Exploiting spatial and temporal variation in program implementation, we find that centralization reduced household education subsidies, a key public expenditure in Vietnam. Households responded by increasing out-of-pocket education spending, lowering non-recurrent consumption to offset the decline in public support and maintain enrolment levels. The replication package for this study, including the data, code, and supporting materials necessary to reproduce the reported results, is available here . The authors are responsible for the completeness and accuracy of the replication materials.
journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization

abstract: This paper investigates the peer effects of physical attractiveness on students’ cognitive and non-cognitive outcomes. Utilizing a nationally representative sample of Chinese middle school students with random class assignment, we find that exposure to more physically attractive peers is associated with improved academic performance, cognitive skills, and non-cognitive skills. Further analysis reveals that these effects are driven by interactions between male and female students. We provide evidence that these effects operate through improvements in the classroom environment, increased student effort, and enhanced teaching styles, as well as greater teacher responsibility and patience.

abstract: In the context of voting with ranked ballots, an important class of voting rules is the class of margin-based rules (also called pairwise rules). A voting rule is margin-based if whenever two elections generate the same head-to-head margins of victory or loss between candidates, the voting rule yields the same outcome in both elections. Although this is a mathematically natural invariance property to consider, whether it should be regarded as a normative axiom on voting rules is less clear. In this paper, we address this question for voting rules with any kind of output, whether a set of candidates, a ranking, a probability distribution, etc. We prove that a voting rule is margin-based if and only if it satisfies some axioms with clearer normative content. A key axiom is what we call Preferential Equality, stating that if two voters both rank a candidate x immediately above a candidate y, then either voter switching to rank y immediately above x will have the same effect on the election outcome as if the other voter made the switch, so each voter’s preference for y over x is treated equally.
title: Characterizations of voting rules based on majority margins

abstract: We examine the endogenous choice of vertical structure in a setting where downstream firms require two inputs to produce differentiated final products under network externalities. One input is supplied by a common supplier, while the other is provided by a dedicated supplier or produced in-house under vertical integration. Our results are as follows. (i) When the common supplier adopts uniform pricing, vertical integration (vertical separation) emerges as the equilibrium outcome under Cournot competition when network effects are weak (strong). Consequently, vertical separation is Pareto efficient for firms and can maximize consumer surplus and social welfare only when network effects are sufficiently strong. Moreover, a prisoners’ dilemma of vertical integration arises. (ii) Under Bertrand competition, the equilibrium outcome under uniform pricing is exactly the opposite, depending on the strength of network effects. (iii) Finally, when the common supplier engages in price discrimination, vertical integration emerges under Cournot competition, whereas vertical separation emerges under Bertrand competition.
title: Equilibrium vertical structure with common supplier and network externalities

abstract: We consider a general Ramsey model with endogenous discounting, dependent on current consumption or future capital, study the monotonicity properties of the optimal path and propose a new narrative of the existence of a poverty trap, an alternative to the literature on convex-concave production functions. We first demonstrate the continuity and differentiability of the value function, the monotonicity of the policy correspondence and the strict monotonicity of the optimal path. Secondly, to overcome the impossibility of computing the critical capital level that limits the poverty trap, we prove, through two examples where discounting depends either on consumption or on future capital, the existence of a poverty trap for a nonzero-measure set of parameter values.
title: Poverty traps under endogenous discounting

abstract: Social protection programs can affect not only their direct beneficiaries but also other household members, with important implications for human capital investment in low-income settings. In Nepal, where gender disparities in educational investment remain pronounced, additional household resources may reduce these gaps if girls’ schooling is especially vulnerable to tight household budgets. This paper examines whether Nepal’s Old Age Allowance (OAA), a universal non-contributory social pension for older adults, generates such intergenerational effects. Using panel data from the Nepal Household Risk and Vulnerability Survey and a fuzzy regression discontinuity design that exploits the program’s age-70 eligibility cutoff, we estimate the causal effect of OAA receipt on children’s educational expenditure in households near the threshold. We find a marked gender asymmetry: OAA receipt increases annual educational expenditure for female students by about Rs 3802, or roughly 56 percent of the control mean, while the corresponding effect for male students is small and statistically insignificant. The increase for girls is driven mainly by tuition, suggesting that pension income helps households cover the direct costs of formal schooling. Results by recipient gender do not support a simple female-control bargaining channel. Instead, the findings point more toward a financial-constraints interpretation, in which additional resources entering the household through older adults increase spending on daughters’ schooling. More broadly, the paper shows that an untargeted social pension can generate meaningful intergenerational spillovers in children’s education even when it is not designed as an education program, especially in settings where girls’ schooling is more vulnerable to resource scarcity.
title: Beyond generations: Old age allowance and girls’ educational investment in Nepal

abstract: The US administration ties the prices it pays for medicines to those paid abroad and justifies this ‘most-favoured-nation’ policy with the claim that Americans subsidise low prices in Europe. This column describes how the available evidence shows that most-favoured nation risks imposing substantial costs on European health systems for a modest American gain. Moreover, its justification cannot be sustained: lower European prices do not cause higher American ones, and American prices are no benchmark for a fair contribution to innovation. Europe should respond as a Union, close its gap in capital and scale, and coordinate targeted incentives at EU level.
title: Little gain for American patients, real harm for European ones: Why Europe must answer the US' most-favoured-nation pricing as a Union

abstract: Only about two-thirds of US mothers with young children are in the labour force. For many low-income married mothers, taking a job barely pays: most face participation tax rates above 25%, rising to 60% once childcare costs are counted. This column argues that lifting the caps on the childcare credit and basing the Earned Income Tax Credit on the primary earner’s income alone would each raise maternal employment. Together, they could raise it by almost 13 points, from 59% to 72%. Both reforms largely pay for themselves.
title: Making work pay for married mothers: Two simple fixes to US tax credits

abstract: This paper develops a one-period behavioral model of price aggregation in social networks. Investors combine noisy private signals with a centrality-weighted social feed. In the equal-precision benchmark, pricing error is summarized by M = σ 2 H , where H is the Herfindahl concentration of equilibrium signal weights. Greater centrality amplification increases H in non-uniform networks, reducing price informativeness. A Gaussian projection implies larger one-period corrections when pricing error is greater. With heterogeneous precision, centrality-based attention is efficient if and only if visibility weights align with precision weights. The model links network concentration to fragile price discovery.
title: Centrality crowding in asset prices: A limited-attention network model

abstract: This paper estimates the causal effect of a drink-driving conviction on labour market outcomes. Using linked administrative data and variation in the timing of first convictions in a staggered difference-in-differences design, we compare individuals before and after conviction to those convicted later. We find employment falls by 6–7 percentage points and monthly earnings decline by around 2 percent. The effects are driven primarily by reduced job entry as opposed to job loss. Employment effects are largest in industries where employers are more likely to screen applicants for criminal convictions.
title: Costly Misdemeanours: Labour Market Effects of Low-Level Drink-Driving Violations
